title: "Conditional independence"
execute:

Two variables can remain associated even after a third variable is held fixed. [**Conditional independence**](https://www.probabilitycourse.com/chapter1/1_4_4_conditional_independence.php) names the stronger claim that their conditional joint distribution factorizes within every value of the conditioning variable.

We state that factorization, check it within the dative table's conditioning strata, and then distinguish conditional independence from both marginal independence and a causal claim.

## Definition

Let $A$ record recipient pronominality, $B$ recipient realization, and $M$ corpus modality. We write

In the [dative table](poisson-distribution.qmd#the-dative-data), $A$ is
`pronominal` versus `nonpronominal`; $B$ is an NP versus PP recipient; and $M$
is written Wall Street Journal versus spoken Switchboard source. For instance,
the first row is a written *feed* token with a pronominal NP recipient, while a
later *give* row is a written token with a nonpronominal PP recipient. These
codings describe source annotations, not experimental assignments.

$$
A\perp B\mid M
$$

when, for every value with positive conditioning probability,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a,B=b\mid M=m)
=\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid M=m)\,
 \mathbb{P}(B=b\mid M=m).
$$

Equivalently, wherever the conditioning probabilities are positive,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid B=b,M=m)
=\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid M=m).
$$

This equality states the usual conditional-independence criterion: learning $B$ supplies no further information about $A$ after $M$ is known.

For a contingency table within modality $m$, factorization predicts cell count

$$
\widehat n_{ab\mid m}
=\frac{n_{a+\mid m}\,n_{+b\mid m}}{n_{++\mid m}}.
$$

This expected count comes directly from factorization. Multiply
$[n_{a+\mid m}/n_{++\mid m}][n_{+b\mid m}/n_{++\mid m}]$ by the modality total
$n_{++\mid m}$, and one denominator cancels. The result is the row total times
the column total divided by the stratum total.

## Checking factorization in the dative table

The paper analyzes pronominality, modality, and realization jointly with other predictors. The calculation below is a descriptive factorization check, not the paper's fitted model.

```{r}
#| label: dative-conditional-independence
library(ggplot2)

dative <- read.csv(
  "data/english-dative/dative-alternation.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("", "NA")
)

cells <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(dative, dative$modality), function(z) {
  observed <- table(z$recipient_pronominality, z$recipient_realization)
  expected <- outer(rowSums(observed), colSums(observed)) / sum(observed)
  out <- expand.grid(
    pronominality = rownames(observed),
    realization = colnames(observed),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  out$observed <- as.numeric(observed)
  out$expected <- as.numeric(expected)
  out$modality <- z$modality[1]
  out$pearson_contribution <- (out$observed - out$expected)^2 / out$expected
  out
}))

dative$is_np <- as.integer(dative$recipient_realization == "NP")
observed_np <- aggregate(is_np ~ modality + recipient_pronominality,
                         data = dative, FUN = mean)
modality_np <- aggregate(is_np ~ modality, data = dative, FUN = mean)
names(modality_np)[2] <- "expected_np_if_independent"
conditional_plot <- merge(observed_np, modality_np, by = "modality")
names(conditional_plot)[3] <- "observed_np"

discrepancy <- aggregate(pearson_contribution ~ modality, data = cells, FUN = sum)

stopifnot(
  all(cells$expected > 0),
  all(abs(aggregate(observed ~ modality, cells, sum)$observed -
          aggregate(expected ~ modality, cells, sum)$expected) < 1e-10)
)

cells
discrepancy
```

Under conditional independence, the NP proportion would be constant across pronominality values within each modality. The observed values depart from that factorization in both panels.

```{r}
#| label: plot-dative-conditional-independence
#| fig-cap: "Observed NP-recipient proportions and the proportions predicted by conditional independence within modality."
plot_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(modality = conditional_plot$modality,
             pronominality = conditional_plot$recipient_pronominality,
             probability = conditional_plot$observed_np,
             source = "observed"),
  data.frame(modality = conditional_plot$modality,
             pronominality = conditional_plot$recipient_pronominality,
             probability = conditional_plot$expected_np_if_independent,
             source = "conditional-independence reference")
)

ggplot(plot_long, aes(pronominality, probability, group = source,
                      color = source, linetype = source)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.75) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~modality) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("observed" = "grey25",
                                "conditional-independence reference" = "#8B1A1A")) +
  labs(x = "Recipient pronominality", y = "NP-recipient proportion",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A Pearson discrepancy summarizes the departures, but row-level independence is not credible because tokens repeat verbs and spoken speakers. We thus use it descriptively here and do not attach a confirmatory reference claim.

Each `pearson_contribution` is $(n_{ab\mid m}-\widehat n_{ab\mid m})^2/
\widehat n_{ab\mid m}$, so large standardized count discrepancies contribute
more. Summing these values is a compact descriptive lack-of-factorization
score. We do not compare it with a chi-squared reference because the repeated
verbs and speakers undermine the row-independent sampling argument required by
that test.

## Check your understanding

1. Verify one expected cell from its conditional margins.
2. Which graphical pattern would conditional independence produce?
3. Why does conditioning on modality not remove the observed association?
4. Why is a row-independent chi-squared test poorly matched to these data?
5. If the NP proportions were equal across pronominality within each modality,
   would that prove a causal effect was absent?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. For spoken nonpronominal NP recipients, the conditional-independence count is $(475\times1859)/2360=374.163$, compared with 192 observed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Conditional independence would put the two pronominality values at the same NP probability within each modality, so each panel's observed line would be horizontal at its reference line. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Conditioning on modality does not remove the association because the observed NP proportions still differ by pronominality: 0.404 versus 0.884 in speech and 0.541 versus 0.987 in writing. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A row-independent chi-squared reference is poorly matched because corpus tokens repeat verbs and, in the spoken data, speakers. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. No. Conditional independence would be a distributional factorization under
   the represented measure, not a causal conclusion about interventions on
   pronominality or realization.

</details>

Conditional independence requires the joint distribution to factorize within
every modality stratum, and that factorization determines the expected cell
counts. Here the Pearson discrepancy remains descriptive because row
independence is not licensed. The [conditional expectation
page](conditional-expectation.qmd) next asks how mean recipient length changes
with realization.
